titulo: Landing: the biometric queue and the three questions
subtitulo: A camera, four fingerprints, and the three answers that get you waved through

steps.pt: Part 2B. You've landed, you're tired, and the first thing that happens to you in Spain isn't a taxi or a coffee — it's a queue. So let's make it a queue you understand, and give you the three sentences that get you out of it. Warm-up first, ten seconds, because your English rhythm gets worse the more tired you are. Hand on your thigh, one tap per syllable, all the same size: Ma-drid — two taps. Va-ca-cio-nes — four. Flat vowels. Say it, don't slide it.

Here's what's actually happening at that desk. Since April 2026 Europe has been running the Entry/Exit System — EES — across the external border of twenty-nine countries. It replaced the passport stamp. The first time you cross, they read your passport, photograph your face and take four fingerprints. It's free, it isn't a visa, and there is nothing to fill in beforehand. Reported time for a first registration at a self-service kiosk: around four minutes a person. Do that arithmetic for a family of four and you'll understand why people started missing connections in the spring. After the first time your profile is on file and it's quick. And there's a quieter consequence that matters more than the queue: with no stamp, your ninety days are now counted automatically and centrally. 'My stamp was smudged' has stopped being a defence.

Now the genuinely useful bit, because it is not the same at every airport or even on every day. Spain is allowed to run a hybrid — kiosks when it's calm, old-fashioned staffed booths when it isn't — so read the signs instead of guessing which queue you're in. If the sign says 'Autoservicio', that's self-service: passport on the reader, look at the camera, fingers on the glass, and only then join the queue for an officer. If it says 'Control de pasaportes', that's the booth, and a human does the whole thing. And here's the permission, because nobody tells you this one: if you're travelling with children or with someone with reduced mobility, ask a member of staff. Spanish airports have instructed their front-line people to divert families to a staffed desk when the kiosk queue gets long. You're not jumping the queue. You're doing exactly what they asked for.
👂 sign: passport control — the staffed booth. A human takes the photo and the fingerprints.
👂 sign: self-service — the kiosk. You do it yourself first, then queue for the officer.

Now the talking, and there is far less of it than you're braced for. They almost never ask you anything at all. But when they do, it is always the same three questions: why are you here, how long are you staying, and where are you sleeping. Three answers, learned tonight, and you walk through without doing that guilty face people pull at passport control. Here's the first one.
I'm here on holiday. — starts with a B, because the V does too. Four equal beats in 'va-ca-cio-nes'.

steps.promptPt: The officer looks up from your passport and asks what you're here for. Tell her. Say it now.
steps.pt: I'm here on holiday.
Ten days. — the 'z' is the 'th' of 'think': DYETH. Worth banking now, because that same sound is hiding in half the numbers on every bar bill in Spain.

steps.promptPt: She asks '¿Cuántos días?' — how many days. You're here for ten. Answer her, short. Say it now.
steps.pt: Ten days.

George. Three sounds in these answers where an English mouth gives you away instantly. One: hotel. Not 'HOH-tel'. One punch per word and it lands at the end — oh-TEL. Two: Madrid. Not 'MAD-rid'. mah-DREEDH, punch on the end again, and that final D goes soft, like the 'th' in 'father'. And three, the big one — the J in 'alojo', 'me alojo', I'm staying. That is not an English J. Brits: you have had this sound free your entire life. It's the ch in 'loch'. Loch. A-lo-jo. Americans: think 'Bach', then scrape it a bit harder at the back of the throat. Get the loch right and you stop sounding like someone reading off a card.

steps.es: Me alojo en el hotel Rialto, en Madrid.
steps.pinyin: meh ah-LOH-khoh en el oh-TEL ree-AHL-toh, en mah-DREEDH
steps.pt: I'm staying at the Hotel Rialto, in Madrid.
steps.tts: Me alojo en el hotel Rialto, en Madrid.

steps.promptPt: Third question: where are you staying. Give her the hotel and the city — the Hotel Rialto, in Madrid. Say it now.
steps.es: Me alojo en el hotel Rialto, en Madrid.
steps.pinyin: meh ah-LOH-khoh en el oh-TEL ree-AHL-toh, en mah-DREEDH
steps.pt: I'm staying at the Hotel Rialto, in Madrid.
Here's the booking. — the sentence that ends the conversation, because the screen does the arguing for you.

steps.promptPt: She raises an eyebrow at the hotel name. Don't explain and don't improvise — hold up the booking on your phone and say the line that goes with it. Say it now.
steps.pt: Here's the booking.

What else can they legally ask for? Officially: a return or onward ticket, proof of travel insurance, a hotel booking or the address you're staying at, and evidence you can pay your way — Spain does have a published figure per person per day, and it is a real rule on paper. In practice, a British couple landing in Alicante on a charter flight is almost never asked for any of it. But the whole promise of this course is that you are never the person holding up the queue. So the move isn't a longer sentence — it's a better artefact. Have the hotel booking already open on your phone before you reach the desk, hand it over, say the line, and let the screen do the work. Speaking is slower and riskier than showing.

And now the rule underneath all of it, which catches more British visitors than anything else on this list: ninety days in any one hundred and eighty. Not ninety days a year, and not a fresh allowance every January. The window rolls — from today, count back one hundred and eighty days and add up every day you were anywhere in the Schengen area. Your day of arrival counts, and so does your day of departure, so a long weekend costs you four days, not two. Go over and you're risking a ban of up to three years. Two groups get caught every winter. First, sun-seeking couples who go out in November and drift home in March. And second — this one astonishes people — owners of Spanish property. Having a villa in Marbella buys you no extra days whatsoever. You have exactly the same ninety as the backpacker in the hostel.
I'm here on holiday.

One thing in focus, and it answers a question you'll have in about two hours' time. When you check in at the hotel, reception will ask for a list of things that feels wildly excessive: passport, date of birth, phone number, email address, your full home address, and how you're related to the children. That is not nosiness and it is not a scam. Since December 2024 Spanish law has required every hotel, tourist apartment and car hire desk to collect exactly that list and report it to the police. Refuse, and you don't check in. Hand it over and go and have a beer. And keep today's shape: 'Me alojo en…' — I'm staying at. You swap the ending and it fits any address: me alojo en el hotel Rialto; me alojo en un apartamento, en el centro; me alojo en casa de un amigo. Same frame, any destination.

Part 2B done. You know what the camera and the four fingers are for, you can tell a kiosk queue from a booth queue by reading one word on a sign, and you have the three answers on the tip of your tongue with the booking already open on your phone. Next up is the part where you start actually enjoying yourself: the bar, where the same beer comes at three different prices and nobody tells you. And once more, because this is the most perishable corner of the whole course — rules change. Check the official page before you fly; the link is in the app.

secoes.corpo: The Entry/Exit System has been fully operational at the external Schengen border since 10 April 2026, replacing the passport stamp across 29 European countries. It records your name, document details, facial image, four fingerprints, and every entry and exit — including refusals of entry. It is free and there is no form to fill in. First registration at a self-service kiosk has been reported at roughly four minutes per person, which is why the April rollout produced multi-hour queues at some European hubs before airports adjusted. Subsequent crossings reuse your stored profile and are much faster. Member states are permitted to run a hybrid — kiosks plus legacy stamped booths — and to suspend biometric capture temporarily under exceptional pressure, so what you meet on the day depends on the airport and the hour. Field guides through 2026 have been recommending three hours before a long-haul departure rather than the usual two; treat that as other travellers' advice, not an official rule.

British and American visitors may stay in the Schengen area for up to 90 days in any rolling 180-day period. 'Rolling' is the word people miss: there is no calendar reset. From any given day, look back 180 days and total the days you were inside the area — day of entry and day of exit both count as full days. Since EES removed the stamp, that total is now computed automatically from a central record. Overstaying can bring a ban of up to three years. Owning property in Spain confers no immigration right at all: a villa owner in Marbella has exactly the same 90 days as anyone else. If you want longer, that is a visa question, and it needs sorting out at home, months in advance.

secoes.titulo: Why check-in asks for everything short of your blood type
secoes.corpo: Royal Decree 933/2021 has, since 2 December 2024, obliged Spanish accommodation providers and vehicle hire companies to collect and transmit to the security forces: full name, document or passport number, nationality, sex, date of birth, telephone, email, full home address, number of travellers, and the relationship between them where minors are involved. It applies to hotels, tourist apartments and car hire counters alike, sometimes on a form printed only in Spanish. It is a legal requirement, not a data grab by the property — and if you decline to supply it, they cannot check you in.

'Me alojo en…' means 'I'm staying at…' and takes any kind of address, which makes it the only version of this answer you need to memorise. Say the frame, then drop in your accommodation. If you're asked in the more informal register you'll hear '¿Dónde te alojas?'; from an officer it will be the formal '¿Dónde se aloja?' — and that is one of the three places in Spain where 'usted' is genuinely the right register.

exemplos.es: Me alojo en un apartamento, en el centro.
exemplos.pt: meh ah-LOH-khoh en oon ah-par-tah-MEN-toh, en el THEN-troh — I'm staying in a flat, in the centre.

exemplos.es: Me alojo en casa de un amigo.
exemplos.pt: meh ah-LOH-khoh en KAH-sah deh oon ah-MEE-goh — I'm staying at a friend's house.

secoes.titulo: The other things the border can ask for
secoes.corpo: Spain's published entry requirements allow officers to ask for a return or onward ticket, proof of travel insurance, evidence of sufficient funds, and confirmation of your accommodation or the address where you'll be staying. The funds figure is set at 10% of the Spanish minimum wage per person per day with an overall floor of 90% of it — around €122 a day and roughly €1,099 minimum in 2026 — and is proven with cash, traveller's cheques or a credit card together with a bank statement. In reality this is very rarely requested of British or American arrivals on holiday routes. Know it exists, keep the booking on your phone, and don't build a panic out of it.

_cenaPendente: Half past six in the morning at Barajas, the sign over your head says 'Autoservicio', a camera and a glass plate are waiting, and the officer at the end has three questions and ten seconds for you.
_cenaPendenteMotivo: O VALOR ACIMA É A `cena` PRONTA E MAIS NADA — renomeie o campo `_cenaPendente` para `cena` e apague este `_cenaPendenteMotivo`; não cole os dois numa string só (era assim que estava, e a instrução de renomear teria posto 500 caracteres de comentário em português dentro da declaração). 197 caracteres, dentro do teto de 200 do SCHEMA §4.5. POR QUE AINDA NÃO FOI DECLARADA: `cena` é o gatilho de vigência, e o G4 desta parte reprova por desenho — medido em 2026-07-28, 6.059 chars em 9 clipes de narração = 673 chars/clipe contra o teto de 120, e 9 de 9 clipes acima do teto individual de 320 (456 · 842 · 869 · 379 · 625 · 717 · 821 · 798 · 552). Dry-run com `cena` declarada: exatamente 10 erros, todos G4; G5, G7, G9, G13, G15 e o `gesto` do G16 saem limpos. Passar no G4 exige ~50 clipes de narração no lugar de 9, ou seja regravar a Alice inteira — que é exatamente o que o reuso integral desta parte existe para não fazer. Renomear o campo é a única edição que falta, e ela só é honesta depois que a narração for repartida em clipes novos.
permissao: If you are travelling with children or with someone with reduced mobility, ask a member of staff. Front-line staff have been told to send families to a staffed booth when the kiosk queue gets long. You are not jumping the queue — you are doing exactly what they asked for.
espelho: Arriving with an explanation rehearsed, and pulling that guilty face while you wait to give it, is the bit that reads as odd there. The officer's default is to ask nothing at all, and the traveller with a speech ready is the one who slows the desk down.
frasePiso: Three answers on the tip of your tongue and the booking already open before you reach the desk. Most people who land here rehearse none of it and answer the first question in English.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A member of staff walks down the kiosk queue, looks at the pushchair, and points your family towards a booth with an officer in it.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: We are being pulled out of the line. Something is wrong with our passports.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The border is being run as a hybrid — kiosks when it is calm, staffed booths when it is not — and front-line staff have been authorised to move families and passengers with reduced mobility to a legacy booth once the kiosk queue runs long.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Go, and give the three answers and nothing else. If nobody offers, ask a member of staff yourself.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: A person does the four minutes of fingerprints for you, and you are out of the hall while the kiosk queue is still shuffling.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at an airport running kiosks only that morning — the hybrid is decided airport by airport and hour by hour, so the booth that was open yesterday may not be open today.

fichasCulturais.sinal: At the hotel desk the receptionist asks for your passport, your date of birth, your phone, your email, your full home address, and how you are related to the children.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: That is far more than a hotel needs. Either they are being nosy or this is a data grab and my details are about to be sold.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: It is a legal duty on the property, not a request from it: hotels, tourist flats and car hire counters have had to collect that exact list and pass it to the security forces since December 2024.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Hand it over in one go, with the passport and the home address ready before you reach the desk.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: Check-in takes two minutes instead of ten, and the rest of the evening is yours.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a friend's spare room — the duty falls on the business, so a private host who is not letting the place out asks you for nothing.
